newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian telecoms look to grow on rosy 1996 results.
newsitem.headline: Russian telecoms look to grow on rosy 1996 results.

text.p: Russian telecoms companies, which have had consistently rising profits during the tough years of general economic decline, will see profit growth slow this year, analysts said on Monday.
But improved financing and revenue-enhancing reforms will position them to remain one of Russia's few solid growth areas, they said.
Frozen or declining local tariffs and static volumes on higher long-distance rates have decreased growth potential, said CentreInvest Securities telecoms analyst Anton Inshutin.
"Long-distance rates need to be reduced and local (time-based) charges need to be introduced," he said.

But Alfa Capital telecoms analyst Kristen Burton Steiner said shares in some of the companies remained a good buy despite a squeeze between a diminishing rate of growth in revenues and higher growth rate in costs.
"Their price-earnings ratio make them look vastly overpriced (in comparison to other sectors)...but for both fundamental and momentum reasons I still think they are a good buy."
Russia's biggest phone companies announced higher profits in 1996.
Long distance carrier Rostelekom net profit increased to $265 million from $247 million in 1995, calculated according to international standards.
Local Moscow company MGTS (Moskovskaya Gorodskaya Telefonnaya Set) preliminary pre-tax profits, calculated to Russian standards, rose to 489.08 billion roubles from 300.23 billion.
Northern regional carrier PTS (AO Peterburgskaya Telefonnaya Set) net profits rose to 198.1 billion roubles from 150.8 billion in 1995.
And analysts said telecom revenues were set to expand again in 1997, although more slowly than in past years.
"There's a slowing of the rate of growth but we're still talking a lot of growth. The question is -- is it going to slow to 40 percent or 50 percent?" said Burton Steiner.
Burton Steiner said metering, though crucial to raising revenues in the long-term, was meeting regional resistance. Local calls have traditionally been free of charge in Russia.

"Metering is still a populist issue out in the regions," she said. "They are sure pensioners will get their phones cut off, although when they do the experiments they discover it's actually young people with the purchasing power who talk the most."
The effect on profits of local call metering has created a system of haves and have-nots, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst Ruth Belbin said.
"There is still a very big disparity between regional telecoms -- those that have introduced local charges and those that haven't," she said. "That impacts on their revenues."
Access to financing is also separating companies, raising the possibility that the few who raise funds on international markets would leap ahead with infrastructure rebuilding.
MGTS and Rostelekom plan Eurobond issues this year to upgrade ageing lines and, in Moscow's case, install equipment for metering local calls, which analysts said would be positively received.
"For big names with size and weight (a Eurobond) will provide a very welcome boost to their profile," said Belbin.
"There is probably a danger of overkill because there are so many Russian Eurobonds planned -- but Rostelekom and MGTS should be welcomed by the market," she said.
Many Russian companies have said they plan Eurobonds since Russia has successfully launched dollar- and mark-denominated Eurobonds in the last six months.
MGTS announced plans on Friday to issue a $150 million three- to five-year Eurobond at the end of July or September.
Rostelekom also said recently Merrill Lynch was underwriting a $100 million credit for infrastructure development.
